title: Experience Studying Abroad at Freiburg University
paragraphs: I am 近藤光, a sixth-year student at Nagoya University, who trained for three months at Freiburg University. I have now finished the clerkship and am on a plane heading to Hong Kong, my connection. I was originally planning to sleep to match Japan time, but the cup noodles served on board were so delicious that I kept asking for more, and I woke up full, so for the six hours until arriving in Hong Kong I will write down my own account, recalling what I experienced during the study abroad.

What made me join this program was the idle chat of a teacher in a lecture I took in my fourth year. I have forgotten the details of what kind of class it was, but I remember that in the spare time I heard the story of the study abroad he did in his postdoc days and became very interested. However, I felt a vague anxiety about living overseas and having to work in a setting where Japanese is not understood, and I thought, "I will actually experience what studying abroad is like while I am still a student, when failure is allowed," and I applied for this program. At about that time I was also interested in Nagoya University's Joint Degree Program, so I was very happy when it was decided that I would do a clerkship at Freiburg University, with which that program also has a partnership.

As for the clerkship, I rotated through neurosurgery for the first four weeks. Since I was interested in neurology, I faced the clerkship with the eager intention of absorbing a great deal of knowledge of neuroanatomy from the doctors, but the memorable first day of the clerkship ended with being taught nothing and only observing surgery that I did not understand at all. I was shocked, thinking this was not how it was supposed to be, and I was even gloomy about going to the next day's clerkship, but I was encouraged by the sight of 吉川-san, who happened to be assigned to neurosurgery as the first department and was training with me, taking part actively in the clerkship, and I resolved to ask questions actively whenever I did not understand something. Also, to raise the level of my questions, I reviewed the neuroanatomy I had studied in my second year and prepared by asking beforehand about the next day's operations. As I spent my days like this, I came to understand the content of the operations, and I was able to learn about operations for rare cases such as Focal Cortical Dysplasia, trigeminal neuralgia and cavernous hemangioma. Also, communication with the doctor in charge naturally increased, and in the final week the doctor entrusted me with translating a Japanese paper into English and giving a presentation. Looking back now, it was not much of an assignment, but I felt I had been recognised as a trainee, and it became four weeks in which I thought it was good that I had worked hard.

In mid-April, when the end of the neurosurgery clerkship was in sight, I, who wanted to make full use of the neurology knowledge I had studied until then, came to want to devote the whole three months of study abroad to neuroscience. It had been decided before the study abroad that I would rotate next through ophthalmology and radiology, but while receiving advice from a senior from last year, I walked around the whole Neurozentrum myself, looked for departments that would let me take part in a clerkship, and negotiated with the secretaries of those departments, the secretaries of ophthalmology and radiology, and the staff of the Foreign Office. As a result, a clerkship in neurology was refused, but I succeeded in changing my second department to neuroradiology and my third department to the epilepsy center. The clerkship in neuroradiology was the most enjoyable of the three months of study abroad, so much that I extended the clerkship by two weeks. There was no particular fixed schedule, and the system was that I could freely take part in endovascular treatment and in diagnosis in the MRI and CT rooms, so I could study the fields I was interested in whenever I liked. In endovascular treatment, the main work was treating patients brought in as emergencies, such as stent placement for cerebral infarction and coil embolisation for subarachnoid hemorrhage, and the doctors asked me to assist, and I was allowed to take part in treatment at a pace of about six cases a week. In diagnosis, the work ranged from following up patients with MS and von Hippel-Lindau disease to diagnosing hyperacute stroke, and here too I summarised the imaging findings myself and gave a light presentation in front of the doctor. Sometimes, when I reported correctly, my findings were written into the report, which was very rewarding. Sometimes, early in the morning, together with a neurology doctor I examined the imaging findings and neurological symptoms of a patient brought in with a stroke, and some days I took part in endovascular treatment while staying with the patient.

At the epilepsy center, in cooperation with neurosurgery, psychiatry and neuroradiology, they examined and treated not only epilepsy but also patients whose chief complaints were convulsions or tremor. Because the clerkship here was a short two weeks, I could not learn as much as in the first two departments, but I was able to study the skill of actually watching a convulsion and predicting to which region of the brain the excitation has spread, how to read EEGs, the differentiation of epileptic from psychogenic convulsions, and the classification of epilepsy. Both of the doctors in charge had studied abroad in their postdoc days, so it was also a good opportunity to hear those stories.

I would also like to touch on things other than the clerkship (how to spend vacations). Speaking of studying abroad, taking breaks is of course important too. Perhaps it is something juniors are curious about as well. To state the conclusion, I think Freiburg is well suited as a base for travel. There was Easter vacation in April, and two public holidays each in May and June, and if you combine them with Saturdays and Sundays to take time off, you can also travel abroad. I myself used vacations to go to the Netherlands and Belgium together with the two who went to Lund and 平野-kun who went to Glasgow, and to visit a friend who went to Vienna. Using DB early-bird fares, Flixbus and low-cost airlines well, one can go abroad quite cheaply, which is perhaps an advantage of studying in Europe. Going abroad is fun, but what I personally want to recommend to my juniors is Rock Am Ring, the largest rock festival on the European continent, held at the Nurburgring in Germany. It boasts nearly 100,000 attendees over three days, and the headliners include world-famous bands such as Slipknot, Tool, Slayer, Foo Fighters and Gorillaz. It is held on a June weekend and holiday, with a schedule very easy for people doing clerkships in Europe to attend, so I definitely want my juniors to take part.

To sum up, unlike the clerkships at other universities, at Freiburg University you do not join a local polyclinic group and train with them, nor do you follow a schedule set in advance by the doctor in charge. For those who want to build the clerkship they idealise in a free environment, I definitely recommend studying at Freiburg University. Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to thank Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and the other doctors of the International Collaboration Office, who gave me great support from the preparation for the study abroad until after my return, and the doctors in Freiburg. Thank you very much indeed.
